newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin ready to change clinic, may appear soon.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin ready to change clinic, may appear soon.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin may be about to leave the clinic where he underwent open heart surgery just three days ago and doctors said the Russian president, eager to get back to political life, could even speak in public on Friday.
The medical team which performed the life-giving operation on the 65-year-old Kremlin leader are pleased with the speed of his progress -- he was out of bed and walking on Thursday.
They will examine him on Friday to see if he is well enough to move to more comfortable and familiar surroundings.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who held the formal reins of power for less than 24 hours while Yeltsin was under anaesthetic on Tuesday, said he expected the president to move from the intensive care wing of the Cardiology Research Centre.
"I think Boris Nikolayevich will transfer tomorrow to the Central Clinical Hospital," he told reporters on Thursday.
"That's what the doctors think too."
Yeltsin spent some time preparing for the multiple bypass operation in a suite at the elite hospital in suburban Moscow. He was also treated there after two heart attacks last year.

Renat Akchurin, the Russian surgeon who led the operating team, told NTV television Yeltsin was recovering ahead of schedule and could be ready to talk in public as early as Friday or Saturday, indicating a televised address may be on the cards.

Yeltsin has already chatted privately with Chernomyrdin as well as family and friends. Asked on Thursday when the president would be able to talk about his operation, Akchurin said: "Tomorrow, the day after tomorrow."

In less than a fortnight, Yeltsin could be carrying out most of his presidential duties although doctors say he will have to avoid straining himself too quickly and may need up to a couple of months for a full convalescence.
"I think that somewhere around 10 to 12 days after the operation he could quite easily fulfil the major part of his duties," Akchurin told NTV.

"You're going to see a vigorous leader," Michael DeBakey, the pioneering U.S. surgeon who advised on the surgery, said after meeting Yeltsin on Thursday, adding that the president had heeded doctors' pleas to stay another day in the emergency room.
DeBakey also said the presidential liver did not bear the tell-tale marks of heavy drinking, which Yeltsin has, despite repeated Kremlin denials, been reputed to indulge in.
In fact, the 88-year-old Texan doctor said, the president could even allow himself the odd booze binge if he wanted. But he will have to cut down on fatty Russian sausages.
Sidelined by heart trouble since his reelection in July, Yeltsin seems to have come out of the operating theatre with a renewed appetite for power and politics.

Announcing his return to the fray, he issued a statement on Thursday calling for national unity and reconciliation as his communist opponents marched in cities across the country to mark the 79th anniversary of the Bolshevik revolution.
He issued a decree renaming the November 7 Revolution Day holiday. It is now the Day of Accord and Reconciliation.

Yeltsin hopes the heart surgery will not only save him from a lingering death but inject new life into his presidency -- he won a new four-year term in July -- and let him to push on with the reforms Russia needs after the collapse of the Soviet Union.
"We are one nation. We have one fate, one future," he said. "We have one Russia and we must be together."

The Kremlin, under chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, has been wooing the political centre, drawing in to government moderates from the communist-led opposition which dominates parliament and attempting to end policy muddle by tightening control over the regions from the capital.
